# Āḷavaka Sutta (Snp 1.10 (PTS Snp 31))

**ID:** Snp 1.10 (PTS Snp 31)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Āḷavaka Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āḷavaka Sutta* (Snp 1.10) is the tenth discourse in the *Uragavagga*, the opening section of the *Suttanipāta* [Sutherland 1991]. Set in the haunt of the *yakkha* Āḷavaka near the town of Āḷavī, the narrative depicts an initial challenge wherein the spirit repeatedly commands the Buddha to exit and re-enter his dwelling [Sutherland 1991; Saddhatissa 2013]. When the Buddha declines to leave on the fourth demand, the *yakkha* threatens to scatter his mind, rip open his heart, or fling him across the River Ganges unless he successfully answers his riddles [Sutherland 1991]. The ensuing dialogue employs an *ākhyāna* (ballad) question-and-answer form drawing on ancient Indian gnomic poetry, highlighting themes of ethical conduct, wisdom, and lay morality—notably praising truth (*sacca*), virtue (*dhamma*), resolve (*dhiti*), and generosity (*cāga*) [Piya Tan 2004; Kalupahana 2001; Anandajoti 2010]. In early Buddhist narrative, the conversion of Āḷavaka exemplifies the motif of the reluctant, skeptical demon subdued by the transformative power of the Dhamma [Buswell 2004].

 A later Central Asian adaptation also survives in fragments of the Old Uygur *Daśakarmapathāvadānamālā* (*Ātavakāvadāna*), although its narrative elements diverge significantly from the Pali transmission [Elverskog 1997].

**Sources**

- [Sutherland 1991] Gail Hinich Sutherland, Disguises of the Demon: The Development of the Yakṣa in Hinduism and Buddhism (1991) — Details of the narrative encounter, the threats made by the yakkha, and the parallel in the Yakkha Saṁyutta.
- [Saddhatissa 2013] H. Saddhatissa, Sutta-Nipāta: New Translation from the Pali Canon (2013) — Setting at Āḷavī, translation synopsis, and comparison to the Sūciloma Sutta.
- [Buswell 2004] Robert E. Buswell Jr. (ed.), Encyclopedia of Buddhism (2004) — Analysis of the yakkha's role as a reluctant convert and foil for Buddhist ethical instruction.
- [Piya Tan 2004] Piya Tan, Buddha & His Disciples: Profiles and Perspectives in Self-Discovery (2002, 2004) — Identification of the riddle exchange as belonging to gnomic ballad (ākhyāna) verse.
- [Kalupahana 2001] David J. Kalupahana, Buddhist Thought and Ritual (2001) — Summary of Buddha's replies and the text's function as a paritta protective chant.
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses (2010) — Citations of specific verse teachings regarding four virtues of a faithful householder.
- [Analayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Rebirth in Early Buddhism & Current Research (2018) — Inclusion of the Āḷavaka Sutta within the extended Catubhāṇavārapāḷi collection.
- [Elverskog 1997] Johan Elverskog, Uygur Buddhist Literature (1997) — Information on the Old Uygur Ātavakāvadāna in the Daśakarmapathāvadānamālā and its differences from the Pali text.
